subject: biology

items.q: A food chain is: algae to mayfly larvae to minnow to pike. The pike has no predators in this ecosystem. Which statement about this food chain is correct?
items.correct: The pike is a tertiary consumer.
items.misconception: The minnow is an apex predator.
items.why: In everyday language 'predator' means anything that catches prey, so students treat 'apex predator' as just another word for a hunter rather than as a position in the food chain. Apex predators are carnivores with no predators. An organism that is eaten by another organism is not an apex predator, however it feeds.
items.random_wrong: The mayfly larvae are at level 1.

items.q: An oak tree of biomass 4000 kg supports 3000 caterpillars of total biomass 6 kg, which are eaten by 20 blue tits of total biomass 0.2 kg. Which description of the pyramid of biomass for these data is correct?
items.correct: The oak tree is the widest bar, at the bottom.
items.misconception: The three bars are drawn with equal widths.
items.why: A food chain diagram draws one arrow between each pair of organisms, which suggests that every level simply passes its food on to the next with nothing missing. Only approximately 10% of the biomass from each trophic level is transferred to the level above it, so there is less biomass available at each higher trophic level and fewer organisms can be supported.
items.random_wrong: The oak tree is the narrowest bar, at the bottom.

items.q: Approximately what percentage of the incident energy from light do producers transfer for photosynthesis?
items.why: Two percentages appear close together in this part of the specification, and students remember the numbers themselves without keeping track of which process each one describes. Producers transfer about 1% of the incident energy from light for photosynthesis; only approximately 10% of the biomass from each trophic level is transferred to the level above it. The two figures describe different transfers and are not interchangeable.

items.q: A trophic level contains 6000 g of biomass. Approximately what mass of biomass is transferred to the trophic level above it?
items.why: Two percentages appear close together in this part of the specification, and students remember the numbers themselves without keeping track of which process each one describes. Producers transfer about 1% of the incident energy from light for photosynthesis; only approximately 10% of the biomass from each trophic level is transferred to the level above it. The two figures describe different transfers and are not interchangeable.

items.q: Which statement explains why biomass is lost between one trophic level and the next?
items.correct: Much of the glucose is used in respiration.
items.misconception: The uneaten parts of the prey are the main loss.
items.why: The uneaten remains of an animal, such as bones and fur, are the visible part of the loss, so students overlook the material that is lost after the food has been eaten. Losses of biomass are due to: not all the ingested material is absorbed, some is egested as faeces; some absorbed material is lost as waste, such as carbon dioxide and water in respiration and water and urea in urine.
items.random_wrong: Glucose used in respiration is passed on.

items.q: A trophic level contains 800 g of biomass. The trophic level above it contains 40 g of biomass. What is the efficiency of the biomass transfer between these two levels?
items.why: Students divide the two numbers in whichever order gives a tidy answer, and because the topic concentrates on losses they read 'efficiency' as the size of the loss rather than the size of the transfer. The efficiency of a biomass transfer is the biomass transferred to the level above expressed as a percentage or fraction of the mass available at the level below: 40 divided by 800, multiplied by 100, gives 5%.

items.q: A food chain is: grass to rabbits to foxes. Which statement about this food chain is correct?
items.correct: Far fewer foxes than rabbits are supported.
items.misconception: Similar numbers of rabbits and foxes live here.
items.why: A food chain diagram draws one arrow between each pair of organisms, which suggests that every level simply passes its food on to the next with nothing missing. Only approximately 10% of the biomass from each trophic level is transferred to the level above it, so there is less biomass available at each higher trophic level and fewer organisms can be supported.
items.random_wrong: More foxes than rabbits live here, as foxes hunt.

items.q: In the food chain algae to mayfly larvae to minnow to pike, which organism is at trophic level 1?
items.correct: The algae are at trophic level 1, because plants and algae make their own food and are producers.
items.misconception: Trophic level 1 is the first animal in the food chain, because plants and algae are not counted as a trophic level.
items.why: Food chains are often thought of as 'who eats whom', so students begin counting at the first organism that feeds on something else and treat plants and algae as background rather than as part of the chain. Trophic levels can be represented by numbers, starting at level 1 with plants and algae. Plants and algae make their own food and are called producers, so they are level 1; herbivores that eat them are primary consumers at level 2.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: A pike is a carnivore that eats minnows, and minnows are carnivores that eat mayfly larvae. What type of consumer is the pike?
items.correct: The pike is a tertiary consumer, because it is a carnivore that eats another carnivore.
items.misconception: Any animal that eats meat is a secondary consumer.
items.why: Students memorise the pairing 'carnivore equals secondary consumer' from the level 3 statement and apply it to every meat-eater without checking what that animal actually eats. Carnivores that eat herbivores are called secondary consumers at level 3, but carnivores that eat other carnivores are called tertiary consumers at level 4. Trophic levels are numbered according to how far the organism is along the food chain.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: How does a decomposer take in food from dead plant and animal matter?
items.correct: It secretes enzymes into the environment, and the small soluble food molecules then diffuse into it.
items.misconception: Decomposers take dead matter into their bodies and digest it inside them, in the way an animal does.
items.why: Digestion is first met as something that happens inside a gut, so students assume every organism digests food internally, and they confuse decomposers with animals that feed on dead material. Decomposers break down dead plant and animal matter by secreting enzymes into the environment. Small soluble food molecules then diffuse into the microorganism.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: One oak tree of biomass 4000 kg supports 3000 caterpillars of total biomass 6 kg. Which forms the wider bar in a pyramid of biomass?
items.correct: The oak tree, because the bars represent the relative amount of biomass at each level.
items.misconception: The width of each bar in a pyramid of biomass shows the number of organisms at that trophic level.
items.why: Pyramids of numbers are usually met first and are drawn in the same way, so students carry the counting rule across to pyramids of biomass without noticing that the quantity being represented has changed. Pyramids of biomass are constructed to represent the relative amount of biomass in each level of a food chain, not the number of organisms. Trophic level 1 is at the bottom of the pyramid.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Roughly what proportion of the light energy falling on a plant is transferred for photosynthesis?
items.correct: About 1% of the incident energy from light is transferred for photosynthesis.
items.misconception: Producers transfer most of the light energy that falls on them into biomass.
items.why: Leaves are described as being adapted to absorb light, and students assume that a large leaf area means most of the light that lands on a plant must end up in the plant's biomass. Producers are mostly plants and algae which transfer about 1% of the incident energy from light for photosynthesis. Most of the light misses the leaves, is reflected, or passes straight through them.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: A rabbit uses much of its absorbed glucose in respiration. Is that glucose passed on to a fox that eats the rabbit?
items.correct: No. Glucose used in respiration is not available as biomass for the next trophic level.
items.misconception: Glucose that is used in respiration is still passed on to the next trophic level as biomass.
items.why: Respiration is learned as the reaction that supplies energy for an organism, so students treat it as part of building the body rather than as a process that uses up material. Large amounts of glucose are used in respiration, and carbon dioxide and water are lost from the organism as waste, so this material is not part of the biomass transferred to the level above.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

specSource: AQA GCSE Biology (8461) specification; section 4.7.4 Trophic Levels (biology only)
